extracted.intended_audience: high-school students preparing for the ACT Writing / test-takers seeking essay-scoring strategies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and scoring argumentative essays on the ACT Writing test (40-minute in-test essay), explaining the ACT's four scoring domains and how to meet their requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas and Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores reflect the ability to generate productive ideas and engage critically with multiple perspectives on the given issue. Competent writers understand the issue, the purpose, and the audience, and generate ideas relevant to the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key tasks the essay must accomplish to score well: (1) choose a perspective and state it clearly; (2) compare at least one other provided perspective to your chosen perspective; (3) demonstrate understanding of how the perspectives relate to one another; (4) analyze the implications of each perspective you discuss. Analysis does not require arguing from every perspective, but it must evaluate how correct perspectives are and examine implications/complexities/tensions and underlying values or assumptions. The page contrasts lower-scoring (simplistic, absolute restatement of perspectives) versus higher-scoring (nuanced, contextualized, insightful) treatments and warns that inventing an additional fourth perspective is allowed but not recommended in the 40-minute time limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development and Support
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores reflect the ability to discuss ideas, offer rationale, and bolster an argument; competent writers explain and explore ideas, discuss implications, and illustrate through examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes evidence-based reasoning plus detailed, illustrative examples. To score highly, writers must provide logical reasoning and integrated, specific examples that clarify and deepen the argument (not just general or repetitive statements). Lower-scoring essays show weak, confused, or overly general development; higher-scoring essays provide an integrated line of reasoning and illustration, add qualifications/complications, and expand examples to explain significance. Use concrete, relevant examples tied to the argument rather than vague anecdotes or restatements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores reflect the ability to organize ideas with clarity and purpose; competent writers arrange their essay to show relationships among ideas and guide the reader through the discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organization covers both macro-structure (introduction with thesis, body paragraphs, conclusion) and micro-structure (order within paragraphs, logical progression). Lower scores show rudimentary or inconsistent grouping and weak transitions; higher scores exhibit a clear controlling idea, logical sequencing, unity, and transitions that clarify relationships among ideas. Practical recommendations (Top 5 rules): include an introduction with a thesis, present ideas in logical order, unify the essay with one main idea (don't switch mid-essay), avoid writing the entire essay as one paragraph (use paragraph markers if necessary), and use meaningful transitions between paragraphs rather than just 'first/second/last.' The page gives sample paragraph outlines for lower (basic) vs higher (clear controlling idea repeated and developed in each paragraph) scoring essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language Use and Conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores reflect the ability to use written language to convey arguments with clarity; competent writers employ grammar, syntax, word usage, and mechanics appropriately and adjust style and tone for audience and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This domain includes three nested components: (1) Grammar, Usage, and Mechanics — effective communication in standard written English; some minor errors are allowable if meaning is clear, but pervasive errors lower the score; (2) Sentence Structure — clarity, variety, and correct complex constructions; lack of variety or convoluted sentences reduce scores; (3) Vocabulary and Word Choice — precision and skillful word choice; advanced vocabulary must be used correctly and to clarify ideas (misused advanced words hurt the score). Recommended approach: fix grammar/usage first, then sentence structure, then refine vocabulary. Examples contrast common low-score errors (wrong homophones, run-ons, incorrect abbreviations, repetitive sentence starts) with corrected versions that improve clarity and precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring scale / Mastery levels (raw scores 1–6) and scoring mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: ACT graders assign 1–6 on each of the four domains; two graders score each essay. Domain scores (1–6) from two graders are combined to yield domain scores out of 2–12; the Writing score is calculated by averaging the four domain scores to produce a total ACT Writing score from 2–12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Mastery level descriptors (summary):
• 1 — demonstrates little or no skill: fails to generate an intelligible argument; ideas undeveloped; no organizational structure; language errors pervasive and impede understanding.
• 2 — demonstrates weak/inconsistent skill: weak argument or thesis; incomplete/irrelevant analysis; weak development/support; rudimentary organization; language inconsistent and sometimes impeding.
• 3 — demonstrates some developing skill: responds to multiple perspectives with some clarity; development mostly relevant but simplistic; basic organization; language basic but generally clear; distracting errors may be present.
• 4 — demonstrates adequate skill: engages multiple perspectives with clear thesis; relevant context and recognition of implications/complexities; clear organizational strategy; language conveys argument with clarity; errors rarely impede understanding.
• 5 — demonstrates well-developed skill: productively engages perspectives; precise thesis and thoughtful context; deeper development and qualification; productive organization unified by controlling idea; precise word choice and varied sentences; minor errors do not impede understanding.
• 6 — demonstrates effective skill: critically engages perspectives with nuance and precision; insightful context and analysis of implications/complexities; skillful, unified organization and progression; language use is strategic, precise, and varied; only a few minor errors.
The page uses these descriptors to show how essays differ at score points (examples for 3 vs 6) and advises using the rubric to self-evaluate practice essays. It also notes practical scoring logistics (two graders, domain averaging) and suggests seeking external feedback if the writer cannot reliably self-diagnose grammar/usage issues.
